I'm a musician with good relative pitch and I could at one point tell notes absolutely (back when I was more immersed and in training). My gut feeling from the people I studied with etc. is that it's most likely just repeated exposure over many years, usually from very young. You get to recognise a middle C like I can recognise a specific brand of cologne vs. another, or other such examples in different fields. Just another form of memory.

Edit: for anyone thinking I'm saying absolute and relative are the same - I'm **not**. I'm saying I've seen nothing to suggest they're not simply different levels of memory development, rather than some basic physical difference.

The second example should not assume at all only incredible familiarity with a specific reference note then relative pitch from there (I didn't mean to send anyone down the relative track by choosing a simple example). Everyone I know with perfect pitch has incredible familiarity with a multitude of notes. 

We simply don't have a scientific basis (that I've seen cited) for it being assumed an "ability" beyond memory from vast, repeated exposure. 

I would welcome a scientific basis for establishing "perfect pitch" as an ability beyond memory, if anyone has it.

I'm not arguing relative and absolute are the same thing. None of my posts have argued that, ever. Simply that I've seen nothing to suggest perfect pitch is more than (for example) memory.
